sysd-found-119.title: What DNS was designed to do
sysd-found-119.text: DNS aimed to give one consistent name space that is distributed and cached, useful for many applications, and independent of any one network, protocol or host type. That is the opposite of HOSTS.TXT's single central copy. Names need not contain network identifiers, addresses or routes. The data is distributed with local caches, and creating and deleting names is distributed too. Where there are trade-offs between the cost of acquiring data, update speed and cache accuracy, the data's source controls them. Every item is tagged with a type and a class, so one name space can carry different protocol families' address formats.

sysd-found-206.title: What a domain registrar does
sysd-found-206.text: Only a domain's designated registrar can change or delete its information in the central registry. A registrar is a company or office, accredited by a registry, that manages the reservation of domain names for registrants. Registering a domain creates name server records in the parent zone pointing to the domain's authoritative servers, usually at least two. It does not imply DNS hosting, which most registrars offer as an optional service. To change registrar, the owner unlocks the domain and gets a code from the old registrar that proves the request is genuine. The new registrar must also obtain the holder's express permission.

sysd-found-129.title: Subdomains: splitting a site into sections
sysd-found-129.text: In blog.example.com, blog is the subdomain, example is the primary domain and .com is the top-level domain. A subdomain is an extra part added to a main domain name, and one domain can have several. Websites commonly use them to separate logical sections, as in support.example.com and careers.example.com. Each subdomain can also be delegated to its own manager as a zone of administrative autonomy.

sysd-found-105.title: How a DNS lookup works, step by step
sysd-found-105.text:
Typing google.com into a browser starts a short chain of questions. The answer comes back quickly: lookups average 20-120 milliseconds, according to YSlow.

The browser hands the name to the resolver, the program that does the asking. The resolver asks a root server for the .com TLD server. It asks that server for the domain's authoritative server, the one that gives the actual answer, and queries it. The authoritative server returns the IP address for google.com to the resolver, which passes it back to the browser.

Resolvers work from the rightmost label of the name toward the left. With no cached records, resolution starts at a root server. Roots usually do not answer directly but refer the resolver onward, so a query for www.wikipedia.org is referred to the org servers. The resolver repeats this, following referrals until it receives an authoritative answer. Each host is configured with hints, an initial cache of the known addresses of the root name servers.

Starting every lookup at the root would put a large burden on the roots. There are 13 logical root name servers, with additional copies spread worldwide by anycast addressing. Caches in DNS servers keep the roots to a small fraction of all requests.

sysd-found-106.title: The resolver: DNS's client side
sysd-found-106.text:
A resolver is the client side of DNS, which initiates and sequences the queries that end in a full resolution. It is a program that sits between user programs and name servers, on the same machine as the program it serves. Because it may consult several servers or its cache, it can take from milliseconds to several seconds.

Applications ask the resolver in the local operating system. It answers from its cache of recent lookups if it can, and otherwise queries designated DNS servers, usually the ISP's, set up manually or through DHCP. It stores the result and hands it back to the software that asked.

A recursive resolver is the first stop in a DNS query and a middleman between client and name servers. It answers from cache, or asks a root, then a TLD, then an authoritative server, and replies to the client. ISPs typically provide such servers. Without them, every query would start at the root zone, and each user system would need resolver software capable of recursion.

sysd-found-108.title: DNS caches and the TTL: why changes take time
sysd-found-108.text:
DNS stays fast by remembering. A resolver answers from its cache whenever it can. That removes network delay and name server load from most requests, and caches shared by many users work better than unshared ones. Each stored result carries a TTL that says how long it stays valid. The authoritative server's administrator sets it, from a few seconds to several days or weeks. RFC 1912 gives 1 to 5 days as typical.

A cached record keeps its TTL, which the server counts down every second. At zero the record is purged, and the next query must start resolution again. The price is slow change: a changed record spreads only after all caches expire and refresh. TTLs can be lowered before a change, at the cost of more network traffic.

Even a negative answer can be cached. RFC 1034 limits it by the SOA record's MINIMUM field, though later practice also uses the SOA's own TTL. Browsers often keep their own DNS cache, typically for around one minute, which makes DNS issues harder to debug.

sysd-found-112.title: Spreading load with DNS
sysd-found-112.text:
Ask DNS for the same name from two places and you may get two different answers. That is deliberate. Hostnames and IP addresses need not match one to one, so a single hostname can resolve to many addresses. That gives resilience to failures and spreads load across server instances in an enterprise or across the Internet.

Cloud services and CDNs go further. They translate a name into the address of a server near the user, because different users can receive different answers for the same name at the same time. Assigning nearby servers through DNS is key to faster and more reliable responses, and most major Internet services use it.

Servers may also rotate the order of a record set to balance load, and records of type MX can do the same for mail. The reverse works too. Many hostnames can map to one IP address for virtual hosting, and the Host header of a web request then tells the server which name was asked for.

sysd-found-115.title: How DNS can be attacked
sysd-found-115.text:
DNS was designed without strong security, so its responses can be forged or abused. In cache poisoning, data is fed to resolvers as though it came from an authoritative server. This pollutes the cache with false information and long TTLs, so legitimate requests may be redirected to malicious hosts. The weakness is that DNS responses traditionally carry no cryptographic signature. A fix, covered in {{ref:sysd-found-195}}, adds signed responses. TSIG lets trusted peers verify each other and is commonly used to authorize zone transfers and dynamic updates.

DNS is also often seen as innocuous and passes firewalls. It can leak from private connections, carry malware commands in TXT records, as in DNSMessenger, and be used to exfiltrate data. And lookalike names such as paypal.com and paypa1.com can be indistinguishable in some fonts, an IDN homograph attack that is occasionally exploited in phishing.

sysd-found-107.title: Recursive, iterative and non-recursive queries
sysd-found-107.text:
Who does the legwork in a lookup depends on the kind of query. In a recursive query, the client asks one server, which answers completely by querying other name servers as needed, or returns an error. A simple resolver on a home router typically does this against the ISP's server.

In an iterative query, the resolver asks a chain of servers, each referring it to the next until one can fully resolve the request. For www.example.com that means a root server, then a com server, then an example.com server. In a non-recursive query, no further rounds are needed. The server already has the answer, from its cache or as an authoritative server, or it returns a partial result.

A single resolution may combine all three. Typically a client sends a recursive query to a recursive server that keeps a cache, which issues non-recursive queries and returns a single answer. Bits in the query headers negotiate the use of recursion. RFC 1034 requires name servers to implement the iterative approach, which suits datagram access, and allows the recursive approach as an option.

sysd-found-195.title: DNSSEC: signing DNS answers
sysd-found-195.text:
The original DNS design had no security features, so nothing stopped a forged answer from looking genuine. DNSSEC is a suite of IETF extensions that secures DNS data by adding digital signatures, while keeping backward compatibility. It stops applications accepting forged or manipulated data, such as that created by cache poisoning. It proves where data came from, that a name does not exist, and that data is unaltered. It gives neither availability nor confidentiality: responses are signed, not encrypted.

Each answer from a signed zone carries an RRSIG record, a signature checked with the public key found in a DNSKEY record. NSEC or NSEC3 records give cryptographic evidence that a record does not exist. A security-aware resolver sets the DO flag in its query. Because that flag lives in the EDNS extended flags, all DNSSEC transactions must support EDNS.

Deployment has been slow. The standard had to stay backward compatible, scale and prevent zone enumeration, and it met disagreement over root key ownership and perceived complexity.

sysd-found-200.title: Round-robin DNS: simple load spreading
sysd-found-200.text:
Round-robin DNS is easy to implement and hard to manage. The DNS holds several A records for one name, one per server hosting identical content. Each response permutes the address list, and clients normally try the first address, so successive users reach different servers.

Caches in the DNS hierarchy and client-side address caches make it hard to manage. Some resolvers reorder the list to favor numerically closer networks, which RFC 3484 standardized for IPv6, and a Windows Vista bug on IPv4 once defeated the balancing. It only alternates the order of records and ignores transaction time, server load and congestion. So it suits many uniformly distributed connections to equal servers.

It should not be relied on alone for availability. If a service at one listed address fails, DNS keeps handing out that address, though some desktop clients try alternates after a timeout of up to 30 seconds. Modified DNS servers can poll mirrored servers for availability and load, and temporarily remove a server from the pool until it reports being within specs again.

sysd-found-199.title: DNS cache poisoning: teaching a resolver a lie
sysd-found-199.text:
A resolver that believes a lie repeats it to everyone who asks. DNS cache poisoning, also called DNS spoofing, introduces corrupt data into a resolver's cache so that it returns a wrong answer, such as an attacker's IP address. Poisoning one DNS server affects the users it serves directly and those served by its downstream servers, until the cache entry expires. Victims can land on a fake site for phishing or malware.

In one variant, a vulnerable server caches the extra A record for the target domain's name server from an answer about the attacker's own domain. That lets the attacker resolve queries for the whole target domain.

Many attacks are prevented by being less trusting of other servers and ignoring returned records not directly relevant to the query. Randomizing the source port and the 16-bit nonce, a one-time number, with cryptographically secure random numbers greatly reduces the chance of a successful race attack. But NAT devices may rewrite source ports and remove the randomness. DNSSEC counters the attack with digital signatures.

sysd-found-116.title: Who can read your DNS queries?
sysd-found-116.text: Anyone along the path can read a DNS query. DNS was designed as a public directory with no confidentiality controls. Unencrypted queries and responses therefore allow sniffing, hijacking, cache poisoning and tampering by someone in the middle. Defenses include VPNs, which move resolution to the VPN operator, and proxies or public DNS servers, which move it to a trusted third party. Some public servers support DoH, DoT and DNSCrypt. These fixes are argued over. Critics say that stopping the local network operator from inspecting DNS thwarts corporate security policies and Internet censorship. They also say public servers centralize control of resolution in a few large companies.

sysd-found-128.title: Root servers and TLD servers
sysd-found-128.text:
The root of DNS has only thirteen server addresses, yet behind them stand about 1954 instances. The limit exists because the original DNS limits UDP packets to 512 bytes, and IPv6 addresses need more room, which the EDNS0 extension allows. Each operator runs redundant equipment in many locations using anycast addressing, for better performance and to survive failures.

A root server answers requests for records in the root zone. Otherwise it directs the resolver to the TLD name servers for the domain's extension, such as .com, .net or .org. The root zone file, about 2 MB, lists the authoritative servers for all TLDs. A resolver bootstraps from hints, a small root.hints file of root server addresses, which breaks the circular need to know a root server's address before resolving anything.

A TLD name server maintains information for all domain names sharing an extension, the part after the last dot. It answers with the address of the domain's authoritative server. TLD servers fall into generic TLDs such as .com and .org, and country code TLDs such as .uk and .jp.
